source.authors: Rojas V, Labra A, Valdés JL, Velásquez NA
source.title: Females of the four-eyed frog, Pleurodema thaul (Anura, Leptodactylidae), respond behaviourally to conspecific male scent

value: females spent longer periods in the Y-maze zones with conspecific male scent (water from the aquaria of acoustically stimulated males) than in zones with distilled water; the authors present this as a suggestion that females can respond behaviourally to male scents
units: categorical (time in male-scent arm versus water arm, repeated trials on 10 females)
method: Y-maze double-choice: along the floor of one arm (15 x 10 x 10 cm) a trail of 5 ml of conspecific male-scent solution (water from the aquarium of a male isolated for 10 days in distilled water and played the male advertisement call for one hour in complete darkness on 10 consecutive days; samples stored at 4 C for three days), in the other arm 5 ml of water-control (distilled water per the Abstract); gate lifted and the female's reaction monitored for five minutes; first choice (first arm entered) and permanence time in each arm scored
conditions: wild-sourced: 13 adults (3 males as scent donors, 10 females as test subjects) collected at Puente Negro, central Chile (34 40 S, 70 53 W), transported to the laboratory in Talca and afterwards returned in a healthy condition to their geo-referenced collecting point; collection date not printed; 10 females each tested 6 times (twice with the scent of each of the 3 males) = 60 trials, so trials are repeated measures on 10 females; positions of the two solutions swapped to avoid position bias, no randomisation described; Results statistics (the Results sentence runs to 55 words and is not quoted): females spent more time in the male-scent arm than the control arm (sign test Z = 2.33, p < 0.05); same-sentence null: first arm chosen did not differ between arms ('indiscriminately', one-tailed binomial p = 0.385) although in 80% of the 60 trials females entered the male-scent arm; permanence-time indices did not differ between first and second trials (Mann-Whitney Z = -0.483, p = 0.629) or among the three male donors (Kruskal-Wallis H = 2.736, p = 0.741); no means or medians of permanence time printed; the scent was aquarium water from males after call stimulation, so the paper does not separate male chemical cues from any effect of the calling treatment; single control (distilled water), no heterospecific or female-scent comparator
quote: Our data suggest that females are capable of responding behaviourally to male scents, since they spent longer periods in the zones with male scent, rather than in zones with water.
note: Classification: behavioural_response, permanence of wild-caught females at male-scent versus water control in a Y-maze; the value is limited to what the quoted Abstract sentence says, and the significant permanence-time statistic and the null first-choice result are carried in conditions. source.authors: Haswell PM, Jones KA, Kusak J, Hayward MW
source.title: Fear, foraging and olfaction: how mesopredators avoid costly interactions with apex predators

value: giving-up densities (food left in patches) were significantly higher during the wolf-urine treatment than under the mint control treatment: 14.98 ± 6.94 SD (N = 127) versus 11.16 ± 7.10 SD (N = 68) food pieces left
units: food pieces left in a patch at departure (giving-up density, mean ± SD, N = GUD measures)
method: field giving-up-density experiment with automated cameras: each site had six patches (2 x 3 grid, 60 m apart), each a 14 L bucket half-sunk in the ground holding 20 pieces (80 g) of dog food mixed into 8 L of sieved substrate; day 1 untreated, from day 2 a control of 25 g sand scented with 3 ml peppermint extract on a 15 x 15 cm moss piece 15 cm from the bucket, from day 7 the control was removed and 25 g of commercial wolf-urine granules placed in the same spot for five days
conditions: wild-sourced: free-ranging red foxes in mixed beech (Fagus sylvatica) and fir (Abies alba) forest, Plitvice Lakes National Park, Croatia, July to September 2015; 12 sites attempted, foxes foraged at 3 in the north-west of the park, which were repeated in late August; 195 fox GUD measures; fox individuals could not be identified by pelage markings (the authors rely on sites at least 1.5 km apart for site independence), so the number of foxes is unknown; repeated measures from the same patch and a random effect for patch location in the models; treatment order fixed within each 11-day cycle (day 1 untreated, mint control from day 2, wolf urine from day 7), not randomised, so treatment is confounded with time and patch familiarity; the authors call this a conservative approach (less expectation of a response to wolf urine applied later, when foxes were more familiar with and reliant on the patches); control is mint extract (Asda extra special peppermint extract) on sand, not a no-odour or non-predator-urine control; urine is a commercial product (PredatorPee Wolf Urine Yard Cover Granules), donor wolves not described; Results: significant effect of scent treatment on GUDs (F1,93 = 17.243, P < 0.001); same-section secondary results: total daily visit duration affected by scent (F1,9 = 10.570, P = 0.01; visits longer under mint, 269.14 ± 307.22 SD s, N = 63, than wolf urine, 132.59 ± 212.47 SD s, N = 124); more time in major vigilance (F1,26 = 31.996, P < 0.001), less time foraging (F1,52 = 6.132, P = 0.017) and more time sniffing the ground (F1,44 = 5.381, P = 0.025) under wolf urine (Fig. 2 caption means, mint N = 48 versus urine N = 66: major vigilance 18.83 versus 30.30 per cent, foraging 55.48 versus 44.09, sniffing 6.85 versus 12.48); nulls: soil penetration (P = 0.54), percentage visibility to road (P = 0.17) and moon illumination (P = 0.39) had no effect on GUDs; no independent variable significantly influenced visit frequency or minor vigilance (minor vigilance means 5.88 mint versus 7.48 per cent urine)
quote: GUDs were significantly higher (less food harvested from patches) during wolf urine treatment (14.98 ± 6.94 SD, N = 127) than under the control treatment (mint, 11.16 ± 7.10 SD, N = 68).
note: Classification: behavioural_response, foraging-cost response of wild foxes to commercial apex-predator urine against a mint-odour control; the value is limited to the quoted GUD sentence, the F test and the vigilance, foraging and sniffing results are in conditions, and the fixed control-then-urine order means treatment is not separated from time in the cycle.
